original_value: In most developing countries, a huge proportion of the national food basket is supported by small subsistence agricultural systems. A major challenge to these systems is disease and pest attacks which have a devastating effect on the small-holder farmers that depend on these systems for their livelihoods. A key component of any proposed solution is a good disease surveillance network. However, current surveillance efforts are unable to provide sufficient data for monitoring such phenomena over a vast geographic area efficiently and effectively due to limited resources, both human and financial. Crowdsourcing with farmer crowds that have access to mobile phones offers a viable option to provide all year round real-time surveillance data on viral disease and pest incidence and severity. This work presents a mobile ad hoc surveillance system for monitoring viral diseases and pests in cassava. We present results from a pilot in Uganda where this system was deployed for 76 weeks. We discuss the participation behaviours of the crowds with mobile smartphones as well as the effects of several incentives applied.

result.paraphrase: In many developing countries, small subsistence farming systems supply a large share of the national food basket. These systems are heavily threatened by disease and pest outbreaks, which can devastate smallholder farmers who rely on them for their livelihoods. An effective disease surveillance network is a crucial part of any solution. Yet existing surveillance efforts cannot efficiently and effectively gather enough data to monitor such events across a vast geographic area because human and financial resources are limited. Crowdsourcing through groups of farmers with mobile phones provides a practical way to collect real-time, year-round surveillance data on viral disease and pest incidence and severity. This study introduces a mobile ad hoc surveillance system for tracking viral diseases and pests in cassava. We report findings from a pilot deployment in Uganda that ran for 76 weeks and examine participation patterns among crowds using smartphones, along with the impact of several incentives that were applied.
